title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: Quinta — Gen 5:5 וַיְחִי; judicium interlocutorium
pass_a_gloss: To these let the testimony of Scripture be added: for collecting the sum of the years of Adam's life, Gen. 5:5, not content with those words which in like reckonings it has most constantly used alone, it inserted these two, וַיְחִי, doubtless neither in vain nor rashly: yet to what they pertain I do not see, except that it be hinted that Adam, as the divine threat carried, had not died but had lived; which could not proceed from elsewhere than from the grace of God and the satisfaction of our Lord Jesus Christ. This very thing can also be understood from this, that the sentence passed on Adam in paradise was not definitive, but as it were interlocutory, giving space to the man for repentance, the extreme judgment after death having been deferred, and meanwhile defining the man's condition as somehow middle between the damned and the absolved. Hence it came about that God neither pronounced the man cursed, as he did the serpent, but only the earth. And although by the sentence he sentenced him to bodily death, yet he used a circumlocution and was unwilling to call it death, lest it seem to pertain to the execution of the Law's Threat. That judgment therefore was not the extreme (for this Adam had to undergo after death according to that of the Apostle, it is appointed for men to die once, and after this the judgment, Heb. 9) but one sent ahead of the extreme deferred to another time. See if you will the last of my Theses on the fall of Adam.
pass_b_english: Add Scripture's witness. When Genesis 5:5 totals Adam's years, it is not content with the words it always uses alone in like reckonings; it inserts these two, וַיְחִי—surely neither for nothing nor by chance. I see no point for them except to hint that Adam, as the divine threat would have it, had not died but had lived—and that life could come only from God's grace and our Lord Jesus Christ's satisfaction.

The same follows from the paradise sentence: it was not definitive but, as it were, interlocutory—giving the man room to repent, deferring the last judgment until after death, and meanwhile setting his state somehow between the damned and the acquitted. Hence God did not call the man cursed as he did the serpent, but only the ground. And though the sentence bound him to bodily death, it spoke by circumlocution and would not name it "death," lest it look like executing the Law's threat. So that judgment was not the last (Adam must face that after death, per the Apostle: it is appointed for men to die once, and after that judgment—Heb. 9) but a preliminary to the last, deferred to another time. See the last of my Theses on Adam's fall.
source_text: His accedat Scripturae Testimonium: colligens enim summam annorum vitae Adami Gen. v. vers. 5. non contenta iis verbis, quibus in similibus computationibus solis usa est constantissime, interferuit haec duo, וַיְחִי, proculdubio nec frustra, nec temere: quo tamen pertineant non video, nisi ut innuatur, Adamum, ut ferebat divina comminatio, non fuisse mortuum, sed vixisse; quod aliunde quam a Dei gratia, & Domini nostri Jesu Christi satisfactione proficisci non potuit. Hoc ipsum etiam ex eo potest intelligi, quod sententia Adamo lata in paradiso non fuit definitiva, sed quasi interlocutoria, dans spatium homini ad resipiscendum, dilato post mortem extremo judicio, ac interim conditionem hominis definiens, mediam quodammodo inter damnatum & absolutum. Hinc factum est, ut, neque Deus hominem pronunciaverit maledictum, quemadmodum serpentem, sed terram duntaxat. Et quamvis morti corporeae eum addixerit sententia, tamen circumlocutione usus sit, nec mortem eam appellare voluerit, ne videretur pertinere ad Comminationis legis executionem. Fuit igitur judicium illud, non extremum (hoc enim Adamo post mortem subeundum fuit juxta illud Apostoli, statutum est hominibus ut semel moriantur, postea vero judicium Heb. 9.) sed praemissum extremo in aliud tempus dilato. Vide sis Thesium mearum de lapsu Adami ultimam.
